question: What does the film Moneyball illustrate about resistance to a data-driven change?
evidence:
[S1] MTM_Organizational_Change_Detailed_Revised.pdf — page 17
Movie lens: Moneyball — a change case The film is especially useful for explaining why evidence alone does not eliminate resistance: change also affects identity, power and culture. Billy Beane faces a resource disadvantage and cannot compete by simply copying richer baseball teams. Trigger for change: environmental and performance constraints make the existing approach insufficient. The film introduces a data-based method for valuing players rather than relying only on traditional scouting judgement. Content of change: a new decision process challenges established expertise, routines and criteria. Scouts and other insiders resist the new method and defend long-standing beliefs about what a “good player” looks like. Psychological + organizational resistance: identity, expertise, culture and status are threatened. The new approach gains credibility only when it is repeatedly used and connected to results. Change becomes embedded when systems, decisions and evidence consistently reinforce the new method.
reference: Moneyball illustrates that adopting data-based player evaluation challenges established scouting expertise, routines, culture and status. Scouts resist even when performance pressures make change necessary; repeated use and results help the new approach gain credibility. [S1]

question: How does mixed (m-) adjacency address ambiguity associated with 8-adjacency?
evidence:
[S1] Unit-1 Image Fundamentals.pdf — page 9
Two pixels, p and q, are called m-adjacent (mixed adjacent) if these two pixels are either 4-adjacent or diagonal adjacent but not both. m-adjacency is an improvement over 8-adjacency as sometimes 8-adjacency may be ambiguous. Let V be the set of intensity values used to define adjacency. In a binary image, if we are referring to adjacency of pixels with value 1. In a grayscale image, the idea is the same, but set V typically contains more elements. For example, if we are dealing with the adjacency of pixels whose values are in the range 0 to 255, set V could be any subset of these 256 values. We consider three types of adjacency: 1. 4-adjacency. Two pixels p and q with values from V are 4-adjacent if q is in the set N4(p). 2. 8-adjacency. Two pixels p and q with values from V are 8-adjacent if q is in the set N8(p). m-adjacency (also called mixed adjacency). Two pixels p and q with values from V are m-adjacent if a. q is in N4(p), or b. q is in ND(p) and the set N4(p) Ո N4(q) has no pixels whose values are from V. Mixed adjacency is a modification of 8-adjacency, and is introduced to eliminate the ambiguities that may result from using 8-adjacency.
reference: Mixed adjacency allows 4-adjacency or diagonal adjacency only when the two pixels do not share a qualifying common 4-neighbor. This reduces ambiguity that can arise with 8-adjacency. [S1]

question: Compare spatial-domain and frequency-domain image enhancement.
evidence:
[S1] Unit- 2 Image Enhancement (Part A)(1).pdf — page 4
Image Enhancement Methods • Spatial domain: • Image plane itself • Image processing methods involve manipulation directly on the pixels in the image • Frequency/Transform Domain • Involves transforming the image into transform domain • Some processing done in transform domain to enhance the image • Image converted back to spatial domain
reference: Spatial-domain enhancement manipulates pixels directly in the image plane. Frequency-domain enhancement transforms an image, processes it in the transform domain, and converts it back to the spatial domain. [S1]

question: How can interface design reduce the user’s memory load?
evidence:
[S1] Unit-6-UID_JIeh32ZBED(1).pdf — page 7
Reduce the User’s Memory Load • Reduce demand on short-term memory. • Establish meaningful defaults. • Define shortcuts that are intuitive. When mnemonics are used to accomplish a system function (e.g., alt-P to invoke the print function. • The visual layout of the interface should be based on a real world metaphor(Image). For example, a bill payment system should use a checkbook and check register metaphor to guide the user through the bill paying process. • Disclose information in a progressive fashion.
reference: The notes recommend reducing demands on short-term memory, using meaningful defaults, providing intuitive shortcuts, applying real-world metaphors and revealing information progressively. [S1]
